page: Vultr vhf-4c-16gb is an x86_64 architecture server belonging to the High Frequency Compute family. It features 4 shared vCPUs mapped to 2 physical Intel cores with hyper-threading enabled. The system is equipped with 16.0 GB of system memory, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. Local storage is bundled and consists of a 384 GB NVMe SSD. The CPU operates at a clock speed of 2.0 GHz and includes 16 MB of L3 cache, with hardware support for AVX, AES, and FMA instructions.

Benchmark data reveals average performance in standard compute tasks, with a stress-ng single-core score of 2411.16 and a multi-core score of 8740.87. Memory performance is mixed; while small-block cached read bandwidth is average at 497.33 GB/sec, large-block uncached read and write bandwidths fall into the weak category at 35.47 GB/sec and 17.49 GB/sec respectively. Cryptographic and compression workloads show some limitations, as evidenced by a weak Passmark CPU encryption score of 2779.75 and a weak single-threaded gzip compression rate of 22.91 GB/sec.

Database operations on this instance are constrained, with Passmark database benchmarks scoring in the weak tier, though Redis SET operations maintain an average throughput of 6.0 million operations per second. Static web serving throughput is also low at 5.46 GB/sec. Given the shared CPU allocation and the balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, this server represents a budget-friendly option for general-purpose workloads, basic web hosting, and lightweight caching layers rather than intensive database or high-throughput serving tasks.
description: Vultr vhf-4c-16gb is an x86_64 general-purpose server from the High Frequency Compute family, featuring 4 shared Intel vCPUs (2 physical cores), 16.0 GB of RAM, and a bundled 384 GB NVMe SSD. Operating at 2.0 GHz, the processor supports AVX and AES instructions. Benchmarks indicate average general compute capabilities, with a stress-ng multi-core score of 8740.87 and a Passmark CPU score of 7697.28. However, memory bandwidth for large uncached blocks is weak, and database operations show performance constraints. This resource profile is qualitatively cost-effective for entry-level applications, development environments, and moderate caching workloads like Redis, which achieves 6.0 million operations per second, rather than high-throughput web serving or intensive data processing.
